description: Desarrollo de software y análisis de información
summary:
We developed a web application to explore the sky using data from SPHEREx, NASA's space telescope that maps the entire sky in 102 infrared colors. The user enters a coordinate or the name of an object, and the application searches for images of that location, aligns them, and displays them in sequence, like a video, to see with the naked eye if something moved between one pass and the next. This is how nearby, cold objects—such as brown dwarfs or a possible Planet X—are searched for.

An animated guide accompanies the exploration: it explains in simple language what the object is, whether it moved, and what its light tells us. Two exploration modes—space exploration and hunting the stars—turn the search into an educational game.

This is important because SPHEREx data is public, yet difficult to use. Our application allows anyone, with no background in astronomy, to participate in the search.
details:
Project Description

Project GIPIS is an interactive and educational web platform designed to bring the latest space science technology closer to the general public, focused primarily on real data from the SPHEREx mission, complemented by historical astronomical catalogs (GAIA, 2MASS/WISE) for image metadata analysis, and imagery from other satellites (WISE mission).

The solution we propose offers different ways to interact with the satellite's information; indirectly, the minigame uses pre-selected satellite images of different space objects to allow the user to analyze movement and light to "Hunt stars"; in "exploration mode," the experience of being the satellite—positioned in space, traversing and analyzing the objects it encounters—is guaranteed; finally, a mode for advanced research, using the satellite's images with the assistance of a bot, allows users to choose where to investigate and make queries about what is seen on screen.

Benefits of Project GIPIS

Translates complex astronomical datasets and catalog metadata into intuitive visual experiences accessible to anyone without prior astrophysics knowledge.

Combines active learning and gamification with direct scientific exploration in a single browser-based platform.

Impact of Project GIPIS

Fosters Citizen Science by training and motivating the general public to inspect multi-epoch astronomical imagery and recognize real phenomena like proper motion and stellar variability.

Inspires STEM curiosity by letting students and enthusiasts experience how astronomers detect celestial objects across modern and historical surveys.

Used in the project:

Languages: Python 3.11/3.12, JavaScript (ES2020, type-checked with TypeScript/JSDoc, no build step), HTML/Jinja2, CSS, SVG, Bash and PowerShell.

Backend: Flask 3.1 with Flask-Smorest, Marshmallow and OpenAPI 3/Swagger, SQLAlchemy with PostgreSQL 16, Flask-Babel (Spanish/English site), Gunicorn and Waitress.

Science stack: Astropy, NumPy, SciPy, astropy-healpix, reproject, astroquery, Matplotlib, Pillow, fsspec/aiohttp (partial reads of SPHEREx images from AWS S3).

Frontend: Aladin Lite (CDS) showing the SPHEREx HiPS. Animated SVG guide characters in vanilla JS, with Rive as an optional upgrade. Unity WebGL integration layer. Node’s built-in test runner.

Data: NASA SPHEREx DR1/QR3 via IRSA (NASA/IPAC) and the AWS Open Data copy (nasa-irsa-spherex), 2MASS, unWISE, Gaia DR3 (ESA), SIMBAD/Sesame (CDS), and the Firefly line list (Caltech-IPAC).

AI: an open-weight LLM (qwen3:14b on Ollama, self-hosted at GIPIS) answers free-form questions only. The main narration is built from templates filled with measured data. Code and docs were written with help from Claude Code (Anthropic).

Infrastructure and hardware: We built our own caching mirror of IRSA because the IRSA cutout service was rejecting about a third of our requests. Blender for the launch-screen video, made from the official SPHEREx 3D model (NASA Eyes). Git/GitHub.

Creativity

Offers three distinct levels of interaction—playing, simulating the satellite's perspective, and conducting bot-assisted research—turning traditional static sky catalogs into an active space hunt.

Factors Considered by the Team

Balancing scientific accuracy with playability by pairing SPHEREx data with historical catalogs (GAIA, 2MASS/WISE) so celestial motion and brightness changes are clearly perceptible.

Maintaining a modular web architecture with bilingual support (English/Spanish) and accessible, responsive design.

Developing the system design primarily aimed at an audience with no prior scientific or technical background.
